notable_absence.finding: This is the fifth page in a row in this batch to discuss RBAC only in the abstract - it is, in fact, the dedicated 'Authorization' overview page, and it STILL names only one worked example (Data Reader) rather than grounding the discussion in the catalogue. Data Reader is deliberately not minted as role:data-reader from this page alone: the sentence 'the Data Reader role features the Read privilege, which is applied to the data of a bucket' is a simplified illustrative example, not a citation of the role's actual documented permission table (which roles.md gives in full, including the Query resource restriction) - minting from the illustrative example risked creating a thinner, less accurate role:data-reader than roles.md's own record would produce. Left for roles.json, where the full table is available as evidence.

cross_component_finding: role:admin and role:ro-admin, minted here from Community Edition's three-fixed-role list, have internal names (`admin`, `ro_admin`) that are IDENTICAL to roles.md's Full Admin (`admin`) and Read-Only Admin (`ro_admin`) roles - not a naming collision but almost certainly the same two roles restated from the edition-gating angle rather than the role-catalogue angle. role:bucket-full-access's internal name (`bucket_full_access`) also matches roles.md's deprecated 'Application Access' role exactly, and roles.md explicitly states 'Versions of Couchbase Server prior to 5.5 referred to this role as Bucket Full Access' and marks it deprecated with 'Do not grant this role to users.' This page, by contrast, presents Bucket Full Access as one of Community Edition's three LIVE fixed roles with no deprecation warning - either this page is stale relative to roles.md's 8.0 content, or Community Edition specifically still relies on the deprecated role as one of its only three options and roles.md's deprecation warning doesn't fully apply to it. This is a genuine, checkable documentation inconsistency worth a docs-issue, not resolved here.
cross_product_finding: The RBAC Concepts glossary (Resource/Privilege/Role/User) is the clearest single piece of evidence in this whole batch for the round's central question. Capella's model, as the registry already has it, is fundamentally a ROLE catalogue (capella-role:*, closed vocabulary of ~10 named roles) crossed with a separate, much larger, independently named PRIVILEGE catalogue (privilege:capella-advanced-access-*, 27 members) - a genuine two-tier system where roles are documented as bundles of independently catalogued privileges. Server's own glossary defines the same four terms (Resource/Privilege/Role/User) but roles.md (the actual catalogue) never names an individual privilege at all - every one of its ~54 role tables lists Resource/Permission/Restriction directly, with permission values drawn from a small closed set of verbs (None/View/All/specific-action-phrases), and nowhere does a named, independently identified 'privilege' entity appear outside three query-family roles that happen to double as the registry's existing privilege:query-select/query-manage-index/query-system-catalog concepts. So Server's own docs state a two-tier Role/Privilege model in the abstract (this page) but the concrete catalogue (roles.md) is actually one-tier: roles ARE the assignable, nameable, documented unit, and 'privilege' mostly stays an unnamed abstraction (Read/Write/Execute/Manage) baked into each role's permission table rather than surfaced as its own catalogued entity. This is the structural mismatch the round's brief predicted, and it is sharper than a simple 'roles vs privileges are named differently' - it's that Capella's model needs and uses two independently enumerable catalogues, while Server's model needs and documents only one, with the second tier staying implicit except in the query family.
